evidence.excerpt:
Agentic systems persist model-visible memory while mutating workspaces, while a runtime,
registry, or approval service may hold authority state outside both. Identical final files can
then require opposite safe actions. We call this thecross-substrate authority gap: decision-
relevant authorization information resides outside the planner-visible workspace or memory state.
Across two controlled mini-benchmark families, three experiments compare planner-observation
augmentation with an execution-time authority check using real Git lineage, durably recorded
agent execution attempts, deterministic oracles, and two model routes. Experiment 1 is a 128-cell
controlled evidence ablation: authority-blind candidate evidence obtains 0/32 final semantic
success, while raw receipts and a typed relation both obtain 32/32. The missing authority
fact accounts for the gain; typed packaging provides no

evidence.excerpt:
Across two benchmark families, all three experiments use held-out semantic templates, real Git
repositories, durably recorded DeepSeek Harness (DSH) source/target attempts, a Workflow Test
Bench (WTB) lifecycle, structured actions, and deterministic executors/oracles. Model outputs are
scored by deterministic oracles. Unknown or invalid outputs remain failures under fixed intention-
to-treat (ITT) denominators. Input plans and evidence closures were frozen before provider calls,
reconstructed under two physical roots, and checked by independent read-only auditors.

evidence.excerpt:
W1 replays all 32 W0 rows through the runtime enforcement operator without a provider call. W0
contains 6/16 unsafe crossed publication intents; W1 executes 0/16 unsafe publications and leaves
all 16/16 crossed cases safe. Among aligned cases, W1 permits and executes every valid publish
intent (12/12) and induces 0/12 denials. Four other aligned rows lack a valid DeepSeek intent. They
count against valid-intent availability, while the valid-intent execution denominator remains 12.
The crossed comparison has six favorable and zero adverse discordances (exact two-sided finite-
matrix p = 0.03125). The paired test characterizes this fixed experimental matrix. Deployment
prevalence requires a separate sampling design.
evidence.explanation: The matched-intent replay results directly validate the enforcement mechanism's safety and availability on the fixed intent set. The paired test and explicit denominators support the causal attribution.
evidence.paraphrase: Experiment 3's execution guard prevents all six fixed unsafe crossed publication intents from becoming effects (0/16 unsafe publications) and permits all 12 valid authorized publish intents (0/12 denials), with six favorable and zero adverse discordances (exact two-sided p = 0.03125).

evidence.excerpt:
OS-inspired agent systems manage context, memory, scheduling, storage, and access control [7, 9];
generalist multi-agent systems already coordinate agents that navigate local files and execute code [2].
Our experiments isolate one operating-layer decision: whether a shared artifact is authorized for a
downstream effect.
Memory governance is rapidly converging on scope, provenance, temporal state, and enforcement.
Collaborative Memory applies dynamic access control to shared fragments [10]; Governed Shared
Memory formalizes leakage, stale propagation, contradiction, and provenance collapse [6]; MemLin-
eage gates sensitive actions using cryptographic derivation lineage [8]; and MAP-Graph combines
typed provenance, hard permission filtering, graded trust, and risk-sensitive action gates [14]. Our
contribution is a controlled cross-substrate publication construction that (i) proves 
[… separate evidence block …]
authority-blind
observational equivalence against workspace-visible Git evidence and identity-bound commit controls,
(ii) decomposes raw facts from typed packaging, and (iii) evaluates enforcement on the exact same
model intent.
Shared-workspace systems address a neighboring concurrency problem. STORM rejects stale
writes using per-agent workspace versions [4], while CoAgent seeks serializable multi-agent mutation
with notification, repair, and undo [5]. Our paired worlds exclude the stale-write race: both writes
succeed and final bytes match; only actor-attempt-scope publication authority differs. PROV-O
and PROV-AGENT model agents, activities, entities, and workflow context for traceability [11, 13];
in-toto binds authorized supply-chain steps to materials and products [12]. LogAct places actions
in a durable shared log before execution and supports voters and recovery [1]. These 
[… separate evidence block …]
foundations
motivate our benchmark for operating-layer authority in agentic systems and its three-experiment
decomposition.

The experiments span two independently constructed four-template families, two model routes,
structured decisions, and deterministic executors. Experiment 3 reuses 32 Experiment 2 intents; its
paired effects leave the planning denominator at 96. The experiments isolate the mechanism under
controlled conditions. Deployment prevalence, broader model and parent–subagent generalization,
and end-to-end security remain open. Planning with the typed relation is negative and model-
dependent. The store and actor/session allocation are trusted; cryptographic signatures, compromise

of the authority database, multi-tenant policy composition, and identity-bound Git attestation at
scale remain future work. Overall, the results motivate validated permits at the mutation boundary;
The Appendix provides reproducibility details.

support_verification.reason: The cited limitations text explicitly acknowledges controlled conditions, deployment prevalence, broader model and parent-subagent generalization, end-to-end security, trusted store and actor/session allocation, and negative model-dependent typed planning results.

positive_signals: The paper introduces the cross-substrate authority gap: decision-relevant authorization information resides outside the planner-visible workspace or memory state, so identical final files can require opposite safe actions.

The paper contributes a formalization of authority-blind observational equivalence, a typed decision relation, and a three-experiment decomposition separating raw authority facts from typed packaging and planning exposure from execution-time enforcement.

The experimental design uses held-out semantic templates, real Git repositories, durably recorded execution attempts, deterministic oracles, frozen input plans, and independent read-only audits across all three experiments.
The matched-intent design in Experiment 3 isolates the execution guard's causal effect by replaying the exact same 32 model-generated first-action intents with zero additional model calls.

Experiment 1 shows raw authority receipts change final semantic success from 0/32 to 32/32 (R0-C0: 32 favorable, 0 unfavorable discordant pairs; exact two-sided p = 4.66e-10), while typed packaging adds no observed planning-accuracy gain over raw receipts.

Experiment 3's execution guard prevents all six fixed unsafe crossed publication intents from becoming effects (0/16 unsafe publications) and permits all 12 valid authorized publish intents (0/12 denials), with six favorable and zero adverse discordances (exact two-sided p = 0.03125).

The paper positions its contribution against memory governance work (Collaborative Memory, Governed Shared Memory, MemLineage, MAP-Graph), shared-workspace concurrency systems (STORM, CoAgent), and provenance standards (PROV-O, PROV-AGENT, in-toto, LogAct).

The paper acknowledges limitations including controlled conditions, deployment prevalence, broader model and parent-subagent generalization, end-to-end security, trusted store and actor/session allocation, and negative model-dependent typed planning results.
